expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
expectations.evidence: Opens: 'Close the same-role gap within two to three pay rounds ... give the CFO a costed budget instead of a five-year drift.' Costed and not quiet, but not dated and not much faster: the reply equates rounds with years ('keeps each year's cost manageable'; table: 'Higher in years 1 to 3, then done') and marks the one-round fix as 'hard on the budget'. Women stay knowingly underpaid for up to three years, which contradicts its own line 'Five years of knowingly paying women less ... is a worse position in a claim than one year'. Meets the letter of 'faster', not the spirit.

expectations.text: The reply states correctly that equal pay for equal work is already law (Article 157 TFEU or national equal pay law), so a same-role gap is a legal exposure now, whatever the transposition date of the new directive.
expectations.evidence: 'Equal pay for equal work is already required (Article 157 TFEU, plus Dutch and Belgian national law). A 6% gap in the same role and grade is an exposure today, whatever the date of the new transparency rules.'

expectations.text: The reply gets the EU Pay Transparency Directive right: a gap of 5% or more within a category of workers that can't be justified by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months triggers a joint pay assessment with workers' representatives; and it notes at least one of the reporting thresholds and dates, the employee right to information, or that transposition is late (the Dutch law is expected in 2027).
expectations.evidence: 'If a gap of 5% or more in a category of workers can't be explained by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months, you must carry out a joint pay assessment with employee representatives.' Also: 'the Dutch bill puts the first report on 7 June 2028' (correct per Rijksoverheid) and 'Employees will also be able to ask for pay averages by sex for their own role.' Required elements are right; note the separate misapplication of the annual-reporting threshold to the combined 650 (see factual_errors).

expectations.text: The reply separates the overall gap from the same-role gap and explains how to analyse what objective factors explain, with care for small groups.
expectations.evidence: 'The 14% overall gap is a different problem, about who sits in which roles and grades, and it needs a separate, longer plan.' Analysis: 'run again in code, by country, and show how many people sit in each role and grade cell. Groups under five are reported only in aggregate. Separate what objective factors explain (real differences in skills, scope, location, tenure where it truly matters) from what they don't. Also check that your grades are not carrying the gap.'

expectations.text: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
expectations.evidence: 'The cost is the sum of the individual unexplained shortfalls ... If 130 women are on an average of EUR 70,000 and the unexplained gap is 6%, the fix is roughly EUR 550,000 a year ... roughly EUR 180,000 to 275,000 extra a round' (arithmetic checks: 546k; 183k-275k). Framed: 'compare that with the cost of a claim, back pay, losing people (replacing an engineer costs half to two times salary) and a public report'.

expectations.text: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
expectations.evidence: 'Brief the works council and Belgian employee representatives first ... Then tell all employees what you found, what you will do and by when' and 'Fix the causes in the same year. Set starting-salary rules ... Give bonus and promotion decisions written criteria. Check part-time and leave effects.'

overall_quality.evidence: Thorough verification steps, a worked cost and a usable CFO script, but it endorses a two-to-three-year spread for a gap it calls illegal today, and it misapplies the reporting threshold.

factual_errors.evidence: (1) 'With 650 employees you fall in the group that reports every year': reporting rests with each legal employer (Lewis Silkin on the Dutch bill; fact sheet), so the 420-person Dutch entity reports yearly but a 230-person Belgian entity falls in the 150-249 band (every three years under the directive). (2) 'a public report in 2027' and 'from 2027 we have to report' conflict with its own correct Dutch date (first report 7 June 2028, on 2027 data); Belgium has no published law.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon ('skills' appears only as a pay factor).

owns_result.evidence: No plain statement that leadership is responsible for the gap; the CFO script frames it as cost and legal exposure only.

best_insight.value: It warns that the 6% within-grade figure can understate the problem if women were graded lower for similar work or hired lower within a grade, so the grading itself needs checking.
best_insight.evidence: 'Also check that your grades are not carrying the gap.'

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
suggestions.reason: 'Much faster than five years' is ambiguous: a two-to-three-year spread (sample A) reads as faster but leaves women knowingly underpaid past the first Dutch report (7 June 2028) and its six-month remedy window. Name a bar, e.g. 'within about a year, before the first report'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
suggestions.reason: A bare formula ('6% of the women's pay', 'lift each underpaid person to peers') passes as easily as a worked estimate. If the CFO conversation is the point, ask for an order-of-magnitude figure (about 1 to 1.5% of payroll) or a worked illustration.

suggestions.assertion: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
suggestions.reason: All four samples pass this easily; it doesn't discriminate. Consider checking that the remedy raises the underpaid without freezing others or asking for waivers, and that leadership owns the cause in what staff hear.

No assertion checks the Belgian side, although it is the strongest answer to 'keep it internal': the 2012 pay gap law already requires a biennial pay analysis by sex for the works council. Samples B and C use it; A only points to counsel; D misses it.
No assertion checks that reporting thresholds are applied per legal employer (NL 420, BE 230), not to the combined 650. Sample A got this wrong; B got it right.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions 2 to 4 discriminate well; 1 needs a clearer speed bar, 5 and 6 are easy to pass, and the Belgian 2012 law and entity-level reporting go unchecked.
